events.credibility_reason: Second-hand only: the 2016/2017 sources were not opened and the supporting check is unpublished code.
Author is unsure his test is correct; Camicia claim rests on unpublished code and unopened sources.

why: The statement is a pure existence question, so an explicit looping deal in the standard game answers all of it: the Casella deal is a witness, scope whole. The 10 Feb 2024 records entry publishes the explicit deal with loop length; a deterministic deal is decisively checkable by simulation, so it is whole/checkable even without argument (it is the deal itself). The arXiv paper was accepted by the Monthly, a journal of record: digested. Andorno et al. independently produce further standard-deck loops: whole/checkable, later. Pre-snapshot items concern other decks (Paulhus reduced decks, 40-card Camicia), a randomised finiteness question, or a finite length record; I read the bullet as the standard 52-card game, as the frozen list (which still listed it open), Casella et al. and the Wikipedia article frame it, so these are variants. Nessler's record is a neighbouring question with no bearing: none. No AI system is named in any event.
doubts: Close call is the Camicia/reduced-deck reading: if 'a game of beggar-my-neighbour' includes 40-card Camicia, the question was answered before 2024; I rejected this because the list treated it as open and the Camicia claims are second-hand. Whether the 10 Feb 2024 records entry counts as a 'written argument' is debatable, but either way both it and the preprint fall after the snapshot. AI absence for Casella et al. rests on arXiv v1 HTML only; the published Monthly text was unread.
